title: Night Watch in the Tea Gardens
description: Wild elephants cross tea estates at night on routes their herds have used for generations. Villages and tea workers now organize night watches with torches and drums, while crops, homes and lives are lost on both sides of the conflict.
document_text: Every monsoon season, herds of Asian elephants move between forest patches that are now separated by tea estates, rice fields and highways. The animals follow corridors their herds have used for generations, and those corridors now run through villages. Tea workers describe nights spent on bamboo platforms, watching the edge of the plantation with torches and drums. When a herd enters, families lose a season of rice in a single night, and houses built close to the forest are damaged. Elephants are also killed, by trains, by electrified fences and by poisoning. The project follows a community watch group that coordinates by mobile phone and guides herds away from homes without harming them. Forest officials have mapped the main crossing points and asked estates to leave strips of land unplanted. The photographs show the watchers, the damaged homes and the herds moving at dusk, and ask whether people and elephants can share a landscape that both need.
reference_summary: Asian elephants still follow old migration routes that now cross tea estates and villages in Assam, causing deaths and crop losses on both sides. A community night watch and mapped crossing corridors are attempts to let people and elephants share the land.

title: Ghost Cats of the High Pastures
description: In the high pastures of Ladakh, snow leopards sometimes kill the goats and sheep that herding families depend on. The project documents predator-proof corrals, a village insurance scheme and the slow change from revenge killing to tolerance.
document_text: Snow leopards are rarely seen, but herding families in the high valleys know them well. A single night in an open stone corral can cost a family a dozen goats, which is a large part of its income. In the past, some herders responded by trapping or poisoning the cats. The project follows three villages that have taken a different path. With support from a local conservation group, families rebuilt their corrals with wire mesh roofs that keep leopards out. A small insurance fund, paid into by the villages and topped up by homestay income from visiting trekkers, compensates families for animals that are still lost. Camera traps placed by young volunteers show that the leopards remain in the valleys. The photographs follow the herders through a winter, from the mesh corrals to the trekkers' guest rooms, and show how tolerance of a predator can be built when its cost is shared.
reference_summary: Snow leopards in Ladakh kill livestock that herding families rely on, which once led to revenge killings. Predator-proof corrals, a village insurance fund and homestay tourism now spread the cost and build tolerance.

title: Roots Against the Storm
description: Women in coastal villages plant mangrove seedlings to rebuild a living barrier against cyclones and storm surges. The forest also shelters crab collectors and honey gatherers, who work close to the territory of Bengal tigers.
document_text: The mangrove forest at the edge of the delta is both a workplace and a shield. When cyclones strike, the dense roots slow the storm surge before it reaches the villages behind the embankments. Years of cutting and shrimp farming have thinned the forest, and the last major cyclones broke embankments that had protected farmland for decades. The project follows a group of women who run a mangrove nursery and replant mudflats each monsoon. Their husbands and sons collect crabs and wild honey deep in the forest, where Bengal tigers still hunt and where every trip carries risk. Rising salinity has made rice farming harder, so the forest has become more important to household income. The photographs move between the nursery, the mudflats at low tide and the narrow channels where the collectors work, and show a community restoring the ecosystem that protects it.
reference_summary: Coastal communities in the Sundarbans are replanting mangroves that protect their villages from cyclone storm surges. The forest also supports crab and honey collectors who work at risk near Bengal tigers.

title: The Wolf and the Shepherd
description: Wolves have returned to the western Alps after a century of absence. Shepherds who move flocks to summer pastures now spend nights beside electric fences and large guard dogs, and the debate over the predator divides mountain towns.
document_text: For most of the last century there were no wolves in these valleys. Protection laws and the abandonment of mountain farms allowed them to return, and packs now live within sight of ski resorts. For shepherds who take their flocks to high summer pastures, the return has changed daily life. Nights are spent close to the animals, inside portable electric fences, with large guard dogs that were unknown to their grandparents. Losses still happen, and compensation payments arrive late. In the towns, the wolf has become a political symbol: for some a sign of a healthy mountain, for others proof that city dwellers decide the rules for rural people. The project follows one shepherd family through a grazing season and also visits the researchers who track the packs with collars. The photographs show the fences at dawn, the dogs at work and the long walks between pastures.
reference_summary: Wolves have returned to the western Alps, and shepherds on summer pastures now rely on electric fences and guard dogs to protect their flocks. The predator has become a symbol in a wider conflict between mountain communities and urban decision makers.

title: White Reefs
description: After a marine heatwave, large parts of the reef turned white. Bajau fishing families who live in stilt villages above the water describe smaller catches and longer trips, while a local group grows coral fragments to restore damaged areas.
document_text: Coral reefs bleach when warm water forces the corals to expel the algae that give them colour and food. After a long marine heatwave, divers found large white areas on reefs that had been healthy a year earlier. Some recovered when the water cooled; others died and were covered by algae. The Bajau, a seafaring people who live in stilt houses built over the water, depend on these reefs for fish. Fishers now travel further to reach productive grounds and return with smaller catches. A local conservation group, working with the marine park, grows coral fragments on underwater frames and transplants them onto damaged areas. Young Bajau divers are trained to maintain the frames. The photographs alternate between the bleached reef, the stilt village and the coral nursery, and connect ocean warming far away with the food on a family's table.
reference_summary: A marine heatwave bleached large areas of reef in Wakatobi, reducing catches for Bajau fishing families. A local coral nursery and trained young divers are trying to restore the damaged reef.

title: Guardians of the Lions
description: Young Maasai men who once proved themselves by hunting lions now work as lion guardians. They track prides, warn herders when lions are near and recover lost cattle, turning a traditional role into conservation work.
document_text: In Maasai communities around the national park, killing a lion was once a rite of passage and a response to attacks on cattle. As lion numbers fell and land was divided into private plots, conservation groups and community elders created a new role. Young warriors are hired as lion guardians. They learn to read tracks, use radio collars and mobile phones, and visit homesteads to reinforce thorn-bush enclosures. When a lion is close to a village, the guardians warn herders and help move cattle. When cattle are lost in the bush, they find them before lions do. The role keeps the status of the warrior while changing its purpose. The project follows two guardians over a dry season, when competition for grass and water brings lions and livestock closer together, and shows how a culture adapts its traditions to protect a species it once hunted.
reference_summary: In Maasai communities near Amboseli, young warriors who once hunted lions now work as lion guardians. They track prides, warn herders and protect cattle, adapting a tradition to support conservation.

title: Locked Pastures
description: Sami reindeer herders face winters when rain freezes over the snow and the animals cannot reach the lichen beneath. At the same time, wind farms and mines take over grazing land, and herders defend their rights in court.
document_text: Reindeer herding is at the centre of Sami life in the far north. In winter the herds dig through the snow to eat lichen. Warmer winters now bring rain that freezes into a hard crust, locking the lichen away, and herders must buy expensive feed or watch animals weaken. At the same time, the land available for grazing is shrinking. Wind farms, mines, roads and holiday cabins cut through migration routes between winter and summer pastures. Herders argue that these projects are approved without their consent, and some cases have reached the highest courts. The project follows a herding family through the year, from the spring migration to the autumn slaughter, and records the knowledge passed between generations about snow, weather and the land. It shows climate change and land use pressing on an Indigenous livelihood from two directions at once.
reference_summary: Sami reindeer herders in northern Norway face icy winters that lock away the lichen their herds eat, while wind farms and mines cut through grazing land. The project follows a herding family and its fight to keep an Indigenous livelihood alive.

title: Threads of the Lake
description: Maya women around the lake weave on backstrap looms using patterns that identify their towns. A cooperative sells their textiles directly, keeping more income in the community and protecting designs from being copied by large brands.
document_text: The patterns woven into a huipil, the traditional blouse, can tell an observer which town its maker comes from. Maya women learn to weave as girls, on backstrap looms tied to a post at one end and to the weaver's waist at the other. A single garment can take months. For years, middlemen bought these textiles cheaply and resold them to tourists and designers, and some patterns were copied by clothing companies without credit or payment. The project follows a women's cooperative that now sells directly online and to visitors, sets fair prices and records the meaning of each design. The cooperative also campaigns for legal protection of collective designs as intellectual property. The photographs show the looms, the dyeing of thread with plants and the meetings where the weavers decide prices together, and present weaving as both heritage and economic independence.
reference_summary: Maya women around Lake Atitlan weave textiles whose patterns identify their towns. A cooperative now sells directly and campaigns to protect their collective designs, turning heritage into economic independence.

title: Living with the Ancestors
description: In Toraja, families may keep a deceased relative at home for months while they save for a funeral that can last several days. Every few years, families clean and re-dress the remains of their ancestors in a ceremony of remembrance.
document_text: In the highlands of Toraja, death is a long process rather than a single moment. A person who dies may be kept at home, treated as someone who is ill, while the family gathers the resources for a funeral that can last several days and involve hundreds of guests. Buffalo are sacrificed and their meat is shared according to old obligations between families. The dead are placed in cliff tombs or carved stone graves, watched over by wooden effigies. In some villages, every few years, families open the graves, clean the remains of their ancestors and dress them in new clothes, a ceremony called ma'nene. The project follows one extended family through a funeral and a ma'nene ceremony. It shows how the rituals bind relatives who have moved to cities back to their village, and how families negotiate the high cost of honouring the dead.
reference_summary: In Toraja, families keep the dead at home until they can afford elaborate funerals, and later clean and re-dress their ancestors' remains in the ma'nene ceremony. The rituals keep scattered families connected to their village.

title: Hunters of the Altai
description: Kazakh nomads in the Altai mountains train golden eagles to hunt foxes in winter. The tradition passes from parents to children, and young women now take part, while festivals bring tourists and new income.
document_text: In the far west of Mongolia, Kazakh families still move with their herds between summer and winter camps. Some of them keep golden eagles, captured young and trained over months to hunt foxes and hares in the snow. The bond between hunter and bird is close: the eagle is kept for about ten years and then released back into the mountains. Knowledge of training, feeding and handling passes from parents to children. In recent years, girls and young women have begun to train eagles, breaking with the expectation that the practice belongs to men. Annual festivals now attract international visitors, which brings income but also pressure to perform the tradition for cameras. The project follows a family through a winter, from the camp to the hunting grounds and the festival, and asks what it means for a nomadic practice to survive by becoming a spectacle.
reference_summary: Kazakh nomads in western Mongolia train golden eagles to hunt in winter, a tradition passed between generations and now taken up by young women. Festivals bring income and visitors, but also pressure to perform the tradition.

title: The River of Millions
description: Millions of pilgrims gather where rivers meet to bathe during one of the largest religious gatherings on Earth. A temporary city of tents, roads and bridges is built on the riverbank and taken down again weeks later.
document_text: Every twelve years, a temporary city appears on the sandy banks where two sacred rivers meet. Pilgrims come from across the country to bathe on auspicious days, believing the water cleanses them. On the busiest days the crowds are counted in tens of millions. Engineers build pontoon bridges, roads, water lines, hospitals and police posts on land that is under water for part of the year, and dismantle them when the festival ends. Ascetics who live apart from society for most of their lives come down from the mountains and lead processions to the water. The project follows a family of pilgrims from a village, a sanitation worker who keeps the camp clean and a group of ascetics. It shows the scale of organisation needed to keep so many people safe, and the personal meaning of a journey that some make only once in a lifetime.
reference_summary: The Kumbh Mela brings millions of pilgrims to bathe where sacred rivers meet, in a temporary city built and removed for the festival. The project follows pilgrims, workers and ascetics to show both the logistics and the personal meaning of the gathering.

title: Speaking It Back
location_name: Rotorua, Bay of Plenty, New Zealand
description: A generation ago few young people spoke the Maori language. Immersion preschools and schools have raised a new generation of fluent speakers, and young parents now raise their children in the language their grandparents were punished for using.
document_text: For much of the twentieth century, Maori children were discouraged or punished for speaking their language at school, and by the 1970s few young people could speak it. Communities responded by creating immersion preschools where elders spoke only the language with toddlers, followed by immersion primary and secondary schools. Today the young people who grew up in those schools are parents themselves, and many raise their children speaking te reo at home. The language appears on television, in music and in government. Challenges remain: there are not enough fluent teachers, and many adults are learning as a second language. The project follows three generations of one family, from a grandmother who lost her language as a child to a granddaughter who dreams in it, and shows language revival as the recovery of identity.
reference_summary: Maori was once suppressed in schools and almost lost among young people, but immersion preschools and schools have produced a new generation of fluent speakers. The project follows three generations of a family recovering their language and identity.

title: Second Life
description: In one of Asia's largest informal settlements, small workshops sort, wash and melt the city's plastic waste into pellets for new products. The recycling economy supports thousands of families but exposes workers to smoke and chemicals.
document_text: Most of the plastic thrown away in the city passes through the hands of informal workers. Waste pickers collect bottles and packaging from streets and dumps and sell them to small workshops, where the plastic is sorted by colour and type, washed, shredded and melted into pellets that factories reuse. Whole lanes are dedicated to a single material. The trade gives thousands of migrant families an income and recovers material that would otherwise be burned or buried. The work is also dangerous: workers handle sharp and contaminated waste without protection, and the smoke from melting plastic fills narrow lanes where children play. Plans to redevelop the settlement into towers threaten to move the workshops out. The project follows a recycling unit from the dump to the factory gate, and asks whether a city can formalise this work without destroying the livelihoods it supports.
reference_summary: Informal workshops in Dharavi recycle much of Mumbai's plastic waste, supporting thousands of families while exposing workers to smoke and contamination. Redevelopment plans threaten the workshops and the livelihoods they provide.

title: Life Under the Heat
description: In dense neighbourhoods, families who live in rooftop rooms face summer temperatures that make sleep and work dangerous. The project documents how residents cope with heat that concrete and traffic make worse every year.
document_text: Concrete, traffic and a lack of trees make the city several degrees hotter than the desert around it. The effect is strongest in dense neighbourhoods, where thousands of families live in small rooms built on rooftops, directly under the sun. In summer, the rooms do not cool down at night. Residents sleep on the roof, wet their sheets, or spend the hottest hours in mosques and shopping centres with air conditioning. Elderly people and outdoor workers are most at risk of heat illness, and hospital admissions rise during heatwaves. Some residents paint roofs white or grow plants in containers to reduce the heat. The project follows a street vendor, a family in a rooftop room and a doctor at a local clinic through the hottest month of the year, and shows extreme heat as an everyday danger rather than a distant forecast.
reference_summary: Dense neighbourhoods in Cairo trap heat, and families living in rooftop rooms face dangerous summer nights. The project follows residents, a vendor and a doctor to show how people cope with rising urban heat.

title: Keys to the Old City
description: In the oldest neighbourhood of the city, long-term residents are being replaced by tourist apartments. Elderly tenants describe evictions and rising rents, while the shops and festivals that held the community together disappear.
document_text: The narrow streets of the old quarter were for centuries home to fishing families, dock workers and small shopkeepers. Over the last decade, many buildings were bought by investors and converted into apartments rented to tourists by the night. Rents for local residents rose beyond what pensions and salaries could pay, and tenants whose contracts ended were asked to leave. Neighbours who had known each other for decades were replaced by visitors carrying suitcases. Grocery shops became souvenir stores, and the neighbourhood festival now has more spectators than residents. The city has introduced limits on new tourist licences, but residents say the change came too late. The project follows an elderly tenant fighting an eviction, a family that moved to the suburbs and a shop owner who stayed, and asks who a historic neighbourhood is for.
reference_summary: Tourist rentals have pushed long-term residents out of Lisbon's old Alfama quarter through rising rents and evictions. The project follows a tenant, a displaced family and a shop owner to ask who the neighbourhood is for.

title: Riders of the Gridlock
description: Motorcycle taxis move millions of commuters through one of the world's most congested cities. When the government banned them from major roads, riders lost their income and passengers lost the only fast way to work.
document_text: In a city where a short trip by car can take hours, motorcycle taxis known as okada weave through traffic and carry millions of passengers a day. For many young men, riding is the only job available, and a motorcycle bought on credit is the basis of a household budget. Authorities say the motorcycles cause accidents and crime, and banned them from major roads and several districts. Riders had their motorcycles seized and crushed. Passengers now walk long distances or wait for crowded buses, and new bus and rail lines reach only part of the city. App-based ride services tried to formalise the trade before the ban. The project follows riders before and after the ban, the commuters who depended on them and the officials who enforce it, and shows the tension between order, safety and survival in a fast-growing city.
reference_summary: Motorcycle taxis carry millions of commuters through Lagos traffic and support many young riders. A ban on major roads cut riders' income and left passengers without fast transport, exposing a conflict between safety and livelihoods.

title: Below the Street
description: Hundreds of thousands of low-income residents live in half-basement flats, with windows at the level of the pavement. When heavy rains flooded these homes and caused deaths, the city promised to phase them out, but tenants have few affordable alternatives.
document_text: Half-basement flats, called banjiha, were originally built as shelters and later rented as cheap housing. Their windows sit at the level of the pavement, so residents see the feet of passers-by and receive little sunlight. They are damp in summer and cold in winter, but they are among the few homes that students, elderly people and low-income workers can afford in an expensive city. During record rainfall, water poured through these windows faster than residents could escape, and people died in their homes. The city announced it would stop permitting new basement homes and help tenants move, but public housing has long waiting lists and rents above ground remain out of reach. The project follows tenants who stayed after the floods, a family that moved and the volunteers who helped clean flooded rooms, and shows climate risk falling hardest on those with the least housing choice.
reference_summary: Low-income residents of Seoul's half-basement banjiha flats were trapped by deadly floods. The city promised to phase the homes out, but tenants have few affordable alternatives, showing how climate risk follows housing inequality.

title: Lines in the Sky
location_name: La Paz and El Alto, Bolivia
description: A network of cable cars links the high plateau city of El Alto with the valley below, turning a journey of an hour by minibus into a quiet ride of minutes. Commuters, vendors and students describe how the lines changed daily life and the map of the city.
document_text: The two cities sit at very different heights: one in a deep valley, the other on the high plateau above it. For decades, workers from the plateau travelled down each morning in crowded minibuses on steep, congested roads. A network of urban cable cars now crosses the gap, with gondolas passing over rooftops, football pitches and markets. A journey that took an hour can take a few minutes, and the fare is affordable. Indigenous Aymara vendors carry their goods to markets in the valley, students reach universities faster, and residents of the plateau feel more connected to the political centre. Critics point to the cost of the system and to minibus drivers who lost passengers. The project rides the lines with commuters at dawn and at night, and shows how a transport project can change how people see their place in a city.
reference_summary: Urban cable cars connect El Alto on the high plateau with La Paz in the valley, cutting hour-long commutes to minutes. Commuters, vendors and students describe how the system changed daily life and their sense of belonging in the city.

title: Waiting in the Camps
description: Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees who fled violence in Myanmar live in crowded camps on the Bangladesh border. Children grow up without formal schooling or citizenship, and families wait for a safe return that does not come.
document_text: Several years after they fled violence in Myanmar, Rohingya families still live in bamboo shelters packed onto hillsides near the border. They are stateless: Myanmar does not recognise them as citizens, and they are not allowed to work or move freely in Bangladesh. Food rations depend on international aid, which has been cut as donor attention moved elsewhere. Children study in learning centres but cannot earn recognised qualifications. Fires and monsoon landslides destroy shelters each year. Some families have risked dangerous boat journeys to reach other countries. The project follows a teacher who runs a learning centre, a family preparing for the monsoon and young people who dream of a future beyond the fence, and shows the long waiting of a people without a country.
reference_summary: Rohingya refugees who fled Myanmar live in crowded border camps in Bangladesh, stateless and dependent on shrinking aid. The project follows a teacher, a family and young people waiting for a future that has not arrived.

title: The Fence in the Orchard
description: Along the administrative line with the breakaway region, fences appear overnight and move further into Georgian-controlled land. Villagers lose orchards and graveyards on the other side, and some are detained for crossing a line they cannot see.
document_text: After a short war, a line of control was drawn between the breakaway region and the rest of the country. In the years since, fences and signs have been installed along that line and, according to villagers, moved forward into their fields. The process is known locally as borderization. Farmers wake to find that half of an orchard now lies on the other side of a wire fence. Families cannot visit graves of relatives in villages they can see from their windows. People who walk across the unmarked line, sometimes while looking for cattle, are detained and fined. International monitors record the changes but cannot stop them. The project follows farmers on the line, a family separated by it and the monitors who patrol it, and shows how a frozen conflict continues to redraw daily life one fence post at a time.
reference_summary: Along Georgia's line with South Ossetia, fences installed after the war keep advancing into villages, cutting farmers off from orchards and family graves. Villagers who cross the unmarked line risk detention.

title: Night Crossing
description: Small boats leave the North African coast at night carrying people who hope to reach Europe. On a small island, rescuers, fishermen and residents receive the survivors, while the sea crossing remains one of the deadliest migration routes in the world.
document_text: The island is closer to Africa than to the European mainland, and for many people trying to reach Europe it is the first land they see. Overcrowded boats, often unfit for the sea, leave the coast at night. Some are intercepted, some sink, and some are reached by coast guard and charity rescue ships. On the island, volunteers hand out blankets and water at the harbour, and fishermen tell of finding bodies in their nets. A reception centre built for a few hundred people sometimes holds thousands. The people who arrive come from many countries and carry stories of war, poverty and abuse in transit. Political debates in Europe about rescue ships and border controls shape what happens at sea. The project follows a rescue crew, a local fisherman and a young man who survived the crossing, and shows a small community at the edge of a continent's migration politics.
reference_summary: Overcrowded boats cross the Mediterranean at night toward Lampedusa, one of the deadliest migration routes. Rescuers, fishermen and residents receive survivors while European politics shapes what happens at sea.

title: Women of the One-Stop Border
description: Women carry fish, maize and second-hand clothes across the border every day in small quantities. A new joint customs post promised faster crossings, but traders describe fees, paperwork and harassment that make small trade hard.
document_text: Thousands of small traders cross this border every day, most of them women. They carry fish, maize, vegetables and second-hand clothes in quantities small enough to carry on the head or a bicycle, and earn the difference in price between two markets. A joint customs post was built so that goods could be cleared once instead of twice, and regional agreements allow small consignments to cross without duty. In practice, traders describe unofficial fees, confusing paperwork and harassment by officials, and many still use informal paths around the post. Some have formed associations to learn their rights and negotiate with customs. The project follows three traders over a week, from the market at dawn to the border and back, and shows how regional trade policy looks from the point of view of the women whose livelihoods depend on it.
reference_summary: Women traders at the Kenya-Uganda border carry small loads of goods across every day to earn a living. Despite a joint customs post and regional rules, they face fees, paperwork and harassment, and some organise to defend their rights.

title: The Invisible Line
location_name: County Fermanagh, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom
description: The border between Ireland and Northern Ireland crosses fields, roads and even farms without any visible mark. After Brexit, farmers and families feared the return of checkpoints that had disappeared with the peace agreement.
document_text: For most people who live near it, the border is invisible: roads cross it dozens of times, and some farms have fields on both sides. It was not always so. During decades of conflict, the border was lined with military checkpoints and closed roads, and memories of that time remain strong. The peace agreement removed the checkpoints, and shared membership of the European Union removed customs checks. When the United Kingdom voted to leave the Union, people on both sides feared that controls would return and that tensions would follow. Political agreements moved most checks to ports, but uncertainty about rules for goods, animals and medicines affected farmers and small businesses. The project follows a farming family whose land crosses the line, a former soldier who once guarded it and young people who have never known a hard border, and shows how a line can matter even when it cannot be seen.
reference_summary: The Irish border is invisible today, but Brexit raised fears that checkpoints removed by the peace process would return. The project follows a cross-border farming family, a former soldier and young people to show what the line still means.

title: One Nation, Two Countries
description: The Mohawk community of Akwesasne straddles the border between Canada and the United States, and also crosses provincial and state lines. Residents pass through customs to visit relatives, go to school or buy groceries within their own territory.
document_text: The community existed long before the international border was drawn through it. Today its territory is divided between two countries, one province and one state, and residents may cross customs several times a day for ordinary errands. A child may live in one country and attend school in another; a family may need different documents to visit relatives a few kilometres away. The community has its own government and police, and it asserts the right of its people to move freely across their traditional lands, a right recognised in old treaties but applied unevenly by border agencies. Disputes over customs posts, smuggling enforcement and identity documents have caused tension for decades. The project follows a school bus route, an elder who carries a community-issued identity card and border officers on both sides, and shows Indigenous sovereignty tested at an international border.
reference_summary: The Mohawk community of Akwesasne is divided by the Canada-US border, so residents cross customs for everyday life within their own territory. The project shows how Indigenous sovereignty and treaty rights collide with international border controls.

title: When the Water Stayed
description: Record monsoon rains left a large part of the country under water for months. Families living on embankments and roadsides waited for the water to drain from villages and fields, while disease spread in the camps.
document_text: Monsoon rains of unusual strength, together with melting glaciers in the north, flooded large areas of the country. In the southern province, water spread across the flat plains and stayed for months, because there was nowhere for it to drain. Millions of people lost their homes. Families moved with their animals onto raised roads and embankments, living under plastic sheets beside the water. Crops of cotton and rice were destroyed, and fields could not be planted for the next season. Waterborne diseases and malaria spread in the camps, and pregnant women struggled to reach clinics. The government and aid groups delivered food and tents, but help reached some areas weeks late. The project follows a family from the day they left their village to the day they returned to rebuild, and connects a local disaster with a global debate about who pays for climate damage.
reference_summary: Record monsoon floods left much of southern Pakistan under water for months, displacing millions and destroying crops. The project follows a family through life on the embankments and the return home, linking the disaster to debates on climate responsibility.

title: After the Earthquake
description: Two powerful earthquakes destroyed much of an ancient city in a single night. Rescue teams searched the ruins for survivors, and in the months that followed families lived in tents and containers while asking why so many buildings collapsed.
document_text: The first earthquake struck before dawn in winter, when most people were asleep. A second, almost as strong, followed hours later. In the old city, apartment blocks collapsed onto the streets, and many historic buildings were lost. Volunteers and rescue teams from many countries dug through the rubble for days, sometimes pulling survivors out long after hope had faded. Survivors slept in cars and tents in freezing temperatures. In the months after, container cities were built on the edge of town, and families waited for permanent homes. Anger grew over construction rules that had been ignored and over amnesties that had allowed unsafe buildings to stand. The project follows a rescue volunteer, a family living in a container and an architect documenting what was lost, and asks how a city can be rebuilt while its residents grieve.
reference_summary: Two powerful earthquakes destroyed much of Antakya, killing many as buildings collapsed. The project follows rescuers, displaced families in container camps and an architect, and examines anger over ignored building rules.

title: The Long Sit-In
description: Tens of thousands of farmers camped on the highways leading into the capital for more than a year to oppose new agricultural laws. Their encampments became small towns with kitchens, libraries and clinics, until the government repealed the laws.
document_text: When new laws were passed to change how crops are sold, farmers feared they would lose guaranteed prices and be left at the mercy of large companies. Tens of thousands of them, many from the northern grain-growing states, drove tractors to the edge of the capital and were stopped at the city's borders. They stayed. Through a cold winter, a hot summer and a deadly wave of the pandemic, the camps on the highways grew into small towns, with community kitchens feeding anyone who came, libraries, clinics and stages for speeches. Women ran farms at home and joined the protest in turns. Hundreds of protesters died during the year, from cold, illness and accidents. After more than a year, the government repealed the laws. The project follows a family that kept its place in the camp throughout, and shows a peaceful protest sustained by organisation and solidarity.
reference_summary: Farmers camped on highways around Delhi for more than a year to oppose new agricultural laws, building camps with kitchens, libraries and clinics. The peaceful protest ended when the government repealed the laws.

title: Summer of Smoke
description: During a long heatwave, wildfires spread across the island and forced the evacuation of villages and holiday resorts. Firefighters, volunteers and residents fought the flames, while tourists waited on beaches and in sports halls.
document_text: After weeks of extreme heat and strong winds, fires broke out in the forested hills of the island and spread toward villages and coastal resorts. Tens of thousands of people, many of them tourists, were evacuated by road and by boat, and spent nights in schools and sports halls. Firefighters worked with water-bombing aircraft, while local volunteers cut firebreaks and protected homes with garden hoses. Farmers lost olive groves and livestock, and the burned forest left hillsides exposed to erosion. Residents said fires had become more frequent and harder to control, and questioned whether the island was prepared. The tourist season, the main source of income, was disrupted at its peak. The project follows a volunteer fire crew, a family that lost its farm and a hotel worker who helped guests escape, and shows how heat and fire are reshaping life in the Mediterranean.
reference_summary: Wildfires driven by a long heatwave forced the evacuation of villages and resorts on Rhodes. The project follows volunteers, a farming family and a hotel worker to show how heat and fire are changing Mediterranean life.

title: The Dry Seasons
description: After several rainy seasons failed in a row, herding families lost most of their cattle, goats and camels. Families walked long distances in search of water and pasture, and children left school as food ran short.
document_text: Pastoralist families in the north of the country measure wealth in animals. When several rainy seasons failed in a row, the grass did not return and water points dried up. Cattle died first, then goats, and even camels, the most resistant animals, weakened. Families walked for days to reach boreholes where hundreds of herds waited. With the animals gone, there was no milk and no income, and many families came to depend on food aid. Children, especially girls, left school to help find water or because families could not pay fees. Conflicts between communities over the remaining pasture became more frequent. Some families have started to keep fewer, hardier animals or to diversify into small trade. The project follows a family that lost most of its herd and shows how a way of life adapted to drought is pushed to its limit by longer and more frequent dry spells.
reference_summary: Successive failed rainy seasons in northern Kenya killed most of the livestock that pastoralist families depend on, leading to hunger, school dropouts and conflict over pasture. The project follows one family as drought pushes their way of life to its limit.

title: The People's Struggle
description: When the country ran out of foreign currency, queues for fuel and cooking gas stretched for days and prices soared. A peaceful protest camp by the sea grew into a national movement that forced the president to resign.
document_text: The country ran out of the foreign currency needed to import fuel, medicine and food. Power cuts lasted for half the day, queues at fuel stations stretched for kilometres and people waited for days to buy cooking gas. Prices doubled, and families skipped meals. Anger turned toward the government, which people blamed for years of debt and mismanagement. Protesters set up a camp on the seafront near the presidential office, with a library, a kitchen and an art space, and called their movement the struggle. People of different religions and ethnic groups joined together. After months of demonstrations, crowds entered the presidential residence and the president fled the country and resigned. The project follows a young protester, a family in a fuel queue and a shop owner through the crisis, and shows how economic collapse turned into a demand for political change.
reference_summary: Sri Lanka's economic collapse caused fuel, gas and food shortages and soaring prices. A peaceful protest camp in Colombo grew into a national movement that forced the president to resign.
